name: Pyridinium chlorochromate
typicalUses: Primary alcohol → aldehyde in dry CH₂Cl₂
Secondary alcohol → ketone
chemoselectivity: Stops at the aldehyde because no water is present to form the hydrate
Tertiary alcohols are not oxidised
pitfalls: Cr(VI) is toxic
Mildly acidic: buffer with NaOAc for acid-sensitive substrates

name: Swern oxidation
typicalUses: Primary alcohol → aldehyde; secondary alcohol → ketone under mild, metal-free conditions
chemoselectivity: Does not over-oxidise aldehydes to acids
Tolerates most other functional groups
pitfalls: The oxidant is activated DMSO (a chlorosulfonium ion); NEt₃ is only the base for the final elimination
Must be kept cold: above about −60 °C side reactions take over
Produces Me₂S (foul smell), CO and CO₂

name: Dess–Martin periodinane
typicalUses: Primary alcohol → aldehyde; secondary alcohol → ketone at room temperature
chemoselectivity: Neutral, fast and very tolerant of sensitive groups
Does not over-oxidise to the carboxylic acid
pitfalls: Releases acetic acid: add NaHCO₃ or pyridine for acid-sensitive substrates
Hypervalent iodine(V) reagent; its precursor IBX can be shock-sensitive

name: Potassium permanganate
context: The outcome depends on conditions: cold, dilute and basic gives the diol; hot or acidic cleaves the C=C bond.
typicalUses: Cold, dilute, alkaline: syn-dihydroxylation of alkenes
Hot or acidic: cleaves C=C; oxidises primary alcohols and aldehydes to carboxylic acids
Alkylbenzene side chain → benzoic acid
chemoselectivity: A side chain is oxidised only if it has a benzylic C–H: tert-butylbenzene is untouched
Hard to stop at the diol except under cold, dilute, basic conditions
pitfalls: Purple MnO₄⁻ → brown MnO₂ (neutral/basic) or colourless Mn²⁺ (acidic)

name: Osmium tetroxide (catalytic, with NMO)
typicalUses: Syn-dihydroxylation of alkenes (Upjohn); asymmetric version with chiral ligands (Sharpless AD)
chemoselectivity: Stereospecific: cis-alkenes give the syn (e.g. meso) diol
Electron-rich alkenes react fastest
Does not cleave the diol (add NaIO₄ for that)
pitfalls: Volatile and very toxic, so used catalytically with NMO to re-oxidise Os(VI)

name: meta-Chloroperoxybenzoic acid
typicalUses: Epoxidation of alkenes
Baeyer–Villiger oxidation of ketones to esters (and cyclic ketones to lactones)
Sulfide → sulfoxide → sulfone; amine → N-oxide
chemoselectivity: Epoxidation is stereospecific (syn); electron-rich alkenes react faster
Baeyer–Villiger migratory aptitude: tertiary alkyl > secondary alkyl ≈ phenyl > primary alkyl > methyl, with retention of configuration
pitfalls: The m-chlorobenzoic acid by-product can open acid-sensitive epoxides: buffer with NaHCO₃
todoVerify: Relative migratory aptitude of secondary alkyl vs phenyl in Baeyer–Villiger (often quoted as comparable)

name: Ozone
context: The products depend on the workup: reductive gives aldehydes, oxidative gives carboxylic acids.
typicalUses: Ozonolysis: cleavage of C=C into two carbonyl compounds
chemoselectivity: Reductive workup (Me₂S, Zn/AcOH or PPh₃) gives aldehydes and ketones
Oxidative workup (H₂O₂) turns the aldehydes into carboxylic acids
pitfalls: Ozonides are explosive: always work them up before isolating

name: Sodium periodate
typicalUses: Cleavage of 1,2-diols into two carbonyl compounds
With catalytic OsO₄ (Lemieux–Johnson): cleaves alkenes like ozonolysis
chemoselectivity: Needs a 1,2-diol (or 1,2-amino alcohol): an isolated alkene is untouched without OsO₄
cis-Diols react faster, via a cyclic periodate ester
pitfalls: Each C–C bond cleaved consumes one equivalent of IO₄⁻

name: Jones reagent
typicalUses: Primary alcohol → carboxylic acid
Secondary alcohol → ketone
chemoselectivity: Water is present, so the aldehyde hydrate is oxidised further to the acid
Tertiary alcohols are not oxidised (orange stays orange)
pitfalls: Strongly acidic: acetals and other acid-sensitive groups are hydrolysed
Orange Cr(VI) turns green Cr(III) as it works

name: TEMPO with bleach (Anelli)
typicalUses: Selective oxidation of primary alcohols to aldehydes
chemoselectivity: Primary alcohols react much faster than secondary ones
The active oxidant is the oxoammonium ion; NaOCl regenerates it, so TEMPO is catalytic
pitfalls: With a co-oxidant such as NaClO₂, the aldehyde goes on to the carboxylic acid
TEMPO itself is a stable nitroxyl radical

name: Hydrogen peroxide
context: Usually an oxidant (H₂O₂/H₂O, E° = +1.78 V). Towards stronger oxidants such as MnO₄⁻ or Cl₂ it is oxidised to O₂ and acts as a reductant (O₂/H₂O₂, E° = +0.70 V).
typicalUses: Oxidative workup of hydroboration (with NaOH)
Oxidation of I⁻, Fe²⁺ and sulfides
Nucleophilic epoxidation of enones (as HOO⁻)
chemoselectivity: As HOO⁻ in base it is a good nucleophile
pitfalls: Disproportionates to O₂ and H₂O, catalysed by MnO₂ or catalase

name: Sulfur dioxide
context: Usually a reductant (oxidised to sulfate), but it oxidises stronger reductants such as H₂S, being reduced to sulfur.
typicalUses: Reduces I₂, acidified MnO₄⁻ and Cr₂O₇²⁻ (decolourising them)
Forms adducts with amines (Lewis acid at S)
chemoselectivity: Towards H₂S it is the oxidant: 2H₂S + SO₂ → 3S + 2H₂O
pitfalls: SO₂ itself has no H to donate; its aqueous solution is acidic because it forms HSO₃⁻ + H⁺

name: Sodium hypochlorite (bleach)
typicalUses: Co-oxidant in TEMPO oxidations
Haloform reaction of methyl ketones
Oxidation of secondary alcohols in acetic acid
chemoselectivity: Methyl ketones are converted to carboxylates plus CHCl₃ (haloform)
pitfalls: Mixing with acid releases Cl₂; mixing with ammonia gives toxic chloramines

name: Potassium dichromate (acidified)
typicalUses: Primary alcohol → aldehyde (distil off as formed) or carboxylic acid (reflux)
Secondary alcohol → ketone
chemoselectivity: Tertiary alcohols are not oxidised: the classic test
pitfalls: Orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ → green Cr³⁺

name: Tollens' reagent
typicalUses: Test for aldehydes: silver mirror
chemoselectivity: Oxidises aldehydes to carboxylates but not ketones
α-Hydroxy ketones such as fructose give a positive test, because they isomerise to aldehydes in the basic solution
pitfalls: Prepare fresh and do not store: aged ammoniacal silver solutions can form explosive silver nitride

name: Selenium dioxide
typicalUses: Allylic oxidation (to allylic alcohols or enones)
Riley oxidation: α-CH₂ of a ketone → 1,2-dicarbonyl
chemoselectivity: Attacks the allylic position, not the C=C itself
pitfalls: Selenium compounds are toxic and malodorous

name: N-Bromosuccinimide
typicalUses: Radical allylic and benzylic bromination (with light or an initiator)
Bromohydrin formation from alkenes in aqueous DMSO
chemoselectivity: Keeps [Br₂] very low, so allylic substitution wins over addition to the C=C
pitfalls: Brominations of C–H are oxidations of carbon; NBS is a source of Br• or 'Br⁺'

name: Iodine
typicalUses: Iodometric titrations
Iodoform test (with NaOH) for methyl ketones and ethanol
chemoselectivity: A mild oxidant: oxidises S₂O₃²⁻ and SO₂ but not Cl⁻ or Br⁻
pitfalls: Dissolves in KI(aq) as I₃⁻ (I₂ acting as a Lewis acid towards I⁻)

name: Bromine
typicalUses: Anti addition to alkenes (via the bromonium ion)
Bromine water test for unsaturation; tribromination of phenol
chemoselectivity: Arenes need a Lewis acid (FeBr₃) unless strongly activated (phenol, aniline)
pitfalls: Decolourisation of bromine water is not specific to C=C: phenols and enols also react

name: Chlorine
typicalUses: Oxidises Br⁻ and I⁻ to Br₂ and I₂ (halogen displacement)
Radical chlorination of alkanes under UV light
chemoselectivity: Stronger oxidant than Br₂ and I₂ but weaker than F₂
pitfalls: Disproportionates in cold NaOH to Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ (and to ClO₃⁻ when hot)

name: Fluorine
typicalUses: The strongest elemental oxidant; oxidises water to O₂
chemoselectivity: Oxidises every other halide ion
pitfalls: Fluorine can only ever be in the −1 oxidation state in compounds (except F₂ itself, at 0)

name: Nitric acid (concentrated)
context: Both a strong acid and an oxidant; which reduction product forms (NO₂, NO, N₂O, NH₄⁺) depends on concentration and on the metal.
typicalUses: Dissolves copper and silver (which do not react with non-oxidising acids)
With H₂SO₄: nitration of arenes via NO₂⁺
chemoselectivity: Concentrated HNO₃ is usually reduced to NO₂; dilute HNO₃ to NO
pitfalls: In nitrating mixture, HNO₃ is protonated by H₂SO₄: there it acts as a base
Passivates Fe, Al and Cr

name: Ceric ammonium nitrate
typicalUses: Removal of p-methoxybenzyl (PMB) ethers
Hydroquinone → quinone
chemoselectivity: A one-electron oxidant: leaves ordinary benzyl ethers alone while removing PMB
pitfalls: Orange Ce(IV) → colourless Ce(III)
todoVerify: Ce(IV)/Ce(III) potential varies strongly with the acid (≈1.44 V in H₂SO₄, ≈1.61 V in HNO₃)
